# Why CSDR?

## What do we want to learn from an environmental mixture?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
### Scientific goals

- Estimate the **joint health effect**
- Learn the **shape** of the response
- Identify **important contributors**
- Find a useful **mixture summary**

\vspace{0.03cm}
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
### The recurring problem {.alert}

Highly correlated exposures, sparse support, and confounding---all at once.

$$
(X_1,\ldots,X_p)\longrightarrow Y
$$
:::
:::

\vspace{0.4cm}

\begin{center}
\muted{Different methods prioritize different scientific goals.}
\end{center}

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
Environmental mixtures are difficult because we are asking several questions at once.
The point of this talk is not that one method replaces every other method; the estimand
and scientific goal should determine the analysis.
-->

## Mixtures methods make different tradeoffs

\scriptsize

| Method | Dimension | What is learned? | Natural strength |
|:--|:--:|:--|:--|
| WQS / qgcomp | $d=1$ | Scalar joint shift | Interpretable effect |
| PCA / PCP | $1<d<p$ | Exposure variation | Pattern discovery |
| BKMR / BART | $d=p$ | Full exposure-response | Nonlinear interactions |
| **CSDR** | **learn $d$** | **Causal response directions** | **Flexible causal summary** |

\normalsize

### Key distinction {.alert}

CSDR learns the structure in exposure $X$ needed to preserve the **causal** exposure-response.

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
These methods answer different questions. qgcomp estimates a common quantile-shift
contrast. BKMR keeps the full exposure vector. PCP is extremely useful for exposure
pattern discovery, including LOD and unusual-event structure, but it does not use Y.
Avoid saying that these methods are "not causal"; emphasize their different estimands.
-->

## Why not always reduce to a scalar? 

## Why not always estimate the full exposure-response?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
### One exposure

Many observations support a curve.

$$
\mu(x_1)
$$
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
### Two exposures

Observations thin across a surface.

$$
\mu(x_1,x_2)
$$
:::

::: {.column width="34%"}
### Many exposures

Most joint exposure combinations are sparse.

$$
\mu(x_1,\ldots,x_p)
$$
:::
:::

### Consequence {.alert}

More dimensions mean harder nuisance estimation, weaker support, and a response surface that is difficult to communicate.

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
Flexible machine learning does not create information in unsupported parts of exposure
space. Dimension reduction is not merely a visualization trick: it can improve the
statistical problem that comes afterward.
-->

## CSDR is similar to a causally supervised PCA

::: {.column width="29%"}
### Exposures

$$
\mu(x)=\mathbb{E}(Y^x)=g(\beta^\top x),
\qquad
\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times d},
\qquad
d\ll p.
$$
:::

\vspace{0.20cm}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="29%"}
### Exposures

$$
X_1,\ X_2,\ \ldots,\ X_p
$$
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
### Causal summary

$$
Z=\beta^\top X\in\mathbb{R}^d
$$
:::

::: {.column width="32%"}
### Flexible response

$$
\mu_\beta(z)=g(z)
$$
:::
:::

### Plain-language target {.alert}

Replace $p$ exposures with $d$ summaries **without losing the causal mean response**.

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
The response need not be linear. The linearity is in the reduction; g remains flexible.
A single-index model is d=1 and a full response surface is d=p. CSDR learns where the
problem lies between those extremes. The output (a loadings matrix) is the same as PCA. 
-->

## Causal directions can differ from associational directions

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Observed regression

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y\mid X=x)
$$

Confounding can create or obscure exposure directions associated with the outcome.

$$
X\longleftarrow C\longrightarrow Y
$$
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Causal response

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y^x)
$$

CSDR seeks directions that preserve the response under interventions on $X$.

$$
X\longrightarrow Y
$$
:::
:::

### The distinction that matters {.alert}

\centering
\Large Association-preserving $\boldsymbol{\neq}$ causal-effect-preserving

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
PCA is outcome-blind, but even supervised SDR is not automatically causal.
Ordinary MAVE preserves E(Y|X), which can be a different surface from E(Y^x).
CSDR adjusts for C before learning the directions.
-->

## A modular two-stage strategy

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="31%"}
### 1. Adjust

Use $(Y,X,C)$ to construct a cross-fitted causal response $\widetilde Y$.

$$
\mathbb{E}(\widetilde Y\mid X)=\mu(X)
$$
:::

::: {.column width="31%"}
### 2. Reduce

Apply sufficient dimension reduction to $(\widetilde Y,X)$.

$$
(\widehat\beta,\widehat d)
$$
:::

::: {.column width="31%"}
### 3. Estimate

Project exposures and estimate the causal response in $d$ dimensions.

$$
\widehat Z=\widehat\beta^\top X
$$
:::
:::

\vspace{0.25cm}

\centering
\method{Causal nuisance estimation} $\longrightarrow$
\method{standard SDR} $\longrightarrow$
\method{reduced causal ERS}

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
The modularity is the implementation advantage. The package supports RA, DR,
pseudo-outcome, and residual-pair transformations. Use DR as the primary workflow
because it is the package default; introduce RA as a lower-cost sensitivity analysis.
-->

## What does the researcher get?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
### Dimension

\centering
\Huge $\widehat d$

\normalsize
How many causal directions are needed?
:::

::: {.column width="32%"}
### Importance

\centering
\Huge $\widehat\lambda_j$

\normalsize
Which exposures contribute to the subspace?
:::

::: {.column width="32%"}
### Response

\centering
\Huge $\widehat\mu(z)$

\normalsize
What is the shape of the joint causal response?
:::
:::

\vspace{0.35cm}

### Subspace importance score {.alert}

$$
\lambda_j=P_{jj},
\qquad
P=\beta(\beta^\top\beta)^{-1}\beta^\top,
\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^p\lambda_j=d.
$$

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
Do not interpret a particular basis when d>1. The subspace is identified, but a basis
can rotate. SIS is basis-invariant, between zero and one, and sums to d. Recommend
bootstrap intervals in practice.
-->

## PFAS application: four exposures summarized in one direction

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="39%"}
\small

**Study:** 305 term births in the Atlanta African American Maternal-Child Cohort (ATL-AA)

**Exposures:** PFOS, PFOA, PFNA, PFHxS

**Selected dimension:** $\widehat d=1$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat Z={}&0.77\,PFOS+0.14\,PFOA\\
             &+0.26\,PFNA-0.56\,PFHxS
\end{aligned}
$$

\textbf{SIS:} PFOS 0.60; PFOA 0.02; PFNA 0.07; PFHxS 0.31
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
![PFAS exposure-response curve from ATL-AA](../../results/jasa-initial-submission/ATL-AA/ers_causal_no_title_main_paper.pdf){width="90%"}
:::
:::

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
The one-dimensional result makes the joint response displayable as a curve.
Emphasize the rug: the central region is much better supported than the extremes.
PFOS contributes most to the subspace and PFHxS acts in the opposite direction.
qgcomp and BKMR reached broadly compatible substantive conclusions, but their
estimands and outputs differ.
-->

## Where CSDR fits in the analyst's toolbox

\small

| If the scientific question is... | A natural starting point is... |
|:--|:--|
| Effect of increasing all exposures by one quantile | qgcomp |
| Flexible response in the original $p$-dimensional space | BKMR / BART |
| Shared exposure patterns, sources, or unusual events | PCP / `pcpr` |
| Lowest-dimensional summary preserving the causal mean | **CSDR / `csdr`** |

\normalsize

### CSDR is especially attractive when {.alert}

A low-dimensional causal structure is scientifically plausible, but neither $d=1$ nor $d=p$ should be imposed in advance.

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
This slide is the fair comparison. Do not pitch CSDR as replacing qgcomp, BKMR, or
PCP. Pitch it as supplying a target that was missing from the toolbox.
-->

# The `csdr` workflow

## Every analysis starts with three objects

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
\scriptsize

```r
library(csdr)

Y <- dat$birth_weight

A_vars <- c("PFOS", "PFOA", "PFNA", "PFHxS")
A <- dat[A_vars]

C <- model.matrix(
  ~ age + bmi + education + tobacco +
    marijuana + sex,
  data = dat
)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
```
:::

::: {.column width="36%"}
### Outcome

$Y$: health endpoint

### Exposures

$A$: continuous mixture

### Confounders

$C$: sufficient adjustment set
:::
:::

\small

\method{Notation bridge:} The package calls the exposure mixture \texttt{A}; this is the $X$ used in the causal framework.

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
Install the development package once with
remotes::install_github("tXiao95/csdr"). The package requires finite numeric inputs
with unique, nonoverlapping column names, so model.matrix handles categorical
covariates. It does not transform exposures or choose the causal adjustment set.
-->

## Fit the causal subspace

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
\scriptsize

```r
learners <- csdr_learners(sl_library = "SL.glm")

fit <- csdr(
  Y = Y, A = A, C = C,
  variants = "DR",
  d = NULL, max_dim = 3,
  L = 5, seed = 42,
  learners = learners,
  keep_nuisance = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```
:::

::: {.column width="34%"}
### What happens

1. Cross-fit nuisance models
2. Construct $\widetilde Y$
3. Run MAVE
4. Select $\widehat d$
5. Return the fitted subspace
:::
:::

\muted{\texttt{DR} is the package default. \texttt{SL.glm} keeps the tutorial fast; use a prespecified richer library for the substantive analysis.}

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
Teach the public high-level interface. With d=NULL, MAVE::mave.dim selects the
dimension; max_dim limits the search. DR uses both an outcome regression and a
generalized propensity score. keep_nuisance=TRUE supports later diagnostics but makes
the saved object larger. Point out the seed and folds because reproducibility matters.
-->

## Inspect dimension and importance before effects

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
\scriptsize

```r
summary(fit)

B_hat <- coef(fit, variant = "DR")
Z_hat <- scores(fit, variant = "DR")

mave <- mave_fits(fit, variant = "DR")
dim_selection <- mave$dimension_selection

Q_hat <- qr.Q(qr(B_hat))
sis <- rowSums(Q_hat^2)
```

\small

\textbf{PFAS SIS:} PFOS 0.60; PFOA 0.02; PFNA 0.07; PFHxS 0.31
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
### Visual placeholder {.alert}

\centering

Dimension CV curve\\
+\\
SIS dot plot with bootstrap intervals
}}
:::
:::

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
Use the package accessors instead of reaching inside the raw MAVE object. The selected
dimension appears in summary(fit), while mave_fits exposes the raw selection object.
The package does not yet export an importance or plotting helper, so SIS and these
graphics remain custom. Stress that raw beta coefficients are not the preferred
importance estimand when d>1.
-->

## Estimate the response in the reduced exposure

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
\tiny

```r
z_grid <- matrix(seq(
  quantile(Z_hat[, 1], 0.05),
  quantile(Z_hat[, 1], 0.95),
  length.out = 50
), ncol = 1)

ers <- estimate_ers(
  Y = Y, A = Z_hat, C = C,
  a_eval = z_grid, estimator = "DR",
  L = 5, seed = 42,
  verbose = FALSE
)

ers$results
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../../results/jasa-initial-submission/ATL-AA/ers_causal_no_title_main_paper.pdf){width="86%"}
:::
:::

\small

\method{Read the rug before the curve:} Uncertainty and causal interpretation are strongest where the reduced exposure has adequate support.

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
estimate_ers does not accept a csdr fit directly: scores(fit) supplies its exposure
input. Explain that the final causal surface is re-estimated after reduction. Build
the plot verbally in three layers: estimate, interval, observed support. If d is
greater than one, use a contour, surface, or prespecified slices rather than silently
discarding dimensions. The ERS intervals condition on the learned score; uncertainty
from learning the direction requires resampling the complete CSDR-to-ERS pipeline.
-->

## A credible analysis includes diagnostics

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
### Check

- Dimension-selection profile
- Distribution and support of $\widehat Z$
- Nuisance-model performance
- RA versus DR sensitivity
- Bootstrap SIS intervals
:::

::: {.column width="51%"}
\tiny

```r
fit_sens <- csdr(
  Y = Y, A = A, C = C,
  variants = c("RA", "DR"),
  L = 5, seed = 42,
  learners = learners,
  verbose = FALSE
)

summary(fit_sens)

outcome_fits <- nuisance_fits(fit, role = "outcome")
gps_fits <- nuisance_fits(fit, role = "gps")
```
:::
:::

\method{Shared folds:} Compare RA and DR dimensions, subspaces, and response curves.

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
CSDR reduces the exposure dimension; it does not remove causal identification
assumptions. Fitting RA and DR together reuses compatible nuisance work and the same
fold assignments. nuisance_fits is available because the primary fit retained those
objects. Actual performance metrics depend on the learner class; there is not yet a
single check(fit) method. Report the adjustment set, preprocessing, learner library,
folds, evaluation support, and full-pipeline uncertainty procedure.
-->

# Takeaways

## When should I use CSDR?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
### Use CSDR when you want

- A **joint causal exposure--response**
- A **data-adaptive dimension**
- A flexible nonlinear response
- Exposure contribution summaries
:::

::: {.column width="41%"}
### CSDR does not replace

- Study design
- Confounder selection
- Positivity assessment
- Sensitivity analysis
:::
:::

### One-sentence takeaway {.alert}

CSDR learns the smallest exposure representation needed to preserve the causal mean response—and `csdr` turns that target into an applied workflow.

<!-- SPEAKER NOTES:
Close by returning to method choice. If the question is a one-quantile joint shift,
qgcomp may be right. If the full p-dimensional surface is the object, use BKMR.
If exposure patterns are the object, use PCP. Use CSDR for a causally sufficient,
data-adaptive summary.
-->

# Questions?

# Appendix

## Identification assumptions

1. **Consistency:** observed outcomes agree with potential outcomes under the observed exposure.
2. **Conditional exchangeability:** $Y^x\perp\!\!\!\perp X\mid C$.
3. **Positivity:** exposure values of interest are supported within levels of $C$.

### Practical reminder {.alert}

Dimension reduction may improve the support problem, but it does not justify extrapolation or repair an inadequate adjustment set.

## Choosing among causal response constructions

\small

| Construction | Main nuisance inputs | Practical role |
|:--|:--|:--|
| RA | Outcome regression | Lower-cost sensitivity analysis |
| DR | Outcome regression + GPS | Package default; robust to one correctly specified nuisance component |
| PO | Outcome regression + GPS | Doubly robust but noisier SDR response |
| RP | Models for $E(Y\mid C)$ and $E(A_j\mid C)$ | Efficient under additive-confounding structure |

\normalsize

\muted{Teach the DR workflow once; use RA as the clearest sensitivity analysis if time permits.}
